runs.text: dirſe dambas as partes no jugar das armas, ou

lines.note: Dirſe completes diuidirſe from f196; its repetition there is a catchword. The two sides separate in fencing, hence jugar rather than lugar.
Na peleja extends the separation sense to fighting generally. This closes hirakiwakareru from the preceding page.
Hirari kururi to describes a quick whirling movement. The adverb is illustrated with a polearm rather than merely translated as speed.
Naginata wo hirari cu-rurito begins the example of swinging the polearm. The physical break falls inside the mimetic expression.
The fighter swings it and attacks without turning his face away. Vomoteuo restores omote wo from the garbled spacing; mauaite is retained as printed rather than normalized to mawashite.

runs.text: Arremete ſem temor meneando a ala-

lines.note: The source label Toſ. precedes charging fearlessly while moving the halberd. Preserve the label's visible spelling rather than guessing a full title.
Barda completes alabarda, and voltas describes turns made with it. The damaged t explains OCR's volras.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſe ver, ou deſapa-

lines.note: Hirari hirari to describes something appearing or disappearing quickly. The repetition belongs to one adverbial expression.

runs.text: recer a couſa de preßa como abano que ſe arre-

lines.note: The comparison is a thrown fan moving out of sight. De preſſa characterizes the rapid appearance or disappearance.
Meſſa completes arremeſſa, the throwing verb. The line is the end of the fan simile, not a new entry.
Hirata and hirada are alternative names for the broad low boat already listed on f196. The reversed order is intentional cross-listing.
A river boat illustrates the low vessel. Fune is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Cugumelos que nacem aos pès das

lines.note: Hiratake denotes mushrooms growing at trees' feet. The headword's t and Portuguese Cugumelos are recovered from the damaged print, with the mushroom gloss supporting the reading.
Aruores completes the habitat phrase, at the bases of trees. The missing r was OCR damage, not a word boundary.

runs.text: O tecer algũa couſa larga como fitas,

lines.note: Hirauchi here is weaving something broad, such as a ribbon. It is separate from the sword-striking sense introduced shortly afterward.
Hirauchi no obi is a broad woven sash or ribbon. Cingi is the beginning of the Portuguese belt word below.

runs.text: douro largo. ¶ Item, O dar de pancha cõ

lines.note: Douro completes cingidouro. Item introduces striking with the flat, with the sword supplied on the following line.
Catana completes the flat-of-the-sword example. It belongs to Portuguese syntax despite being a Japanese loanword.
Hirazaya is a broad scabbard. Bainha supplies the implement meaning without requiring a separate Japanese-script restoration.
Hirazuke means bringing a vessel alongside broadside. Atraueſſada refers to its orientation rather than damage to the vessel.
Hirazuke ni seyo is an imperative to bring it alongside. The Portuguese Chegai likewise addresses the person manoeuvring it.
The boat is brought near by its side. Fune remains an embedded Japanese word eligible for typeface correction.
Hirazuke no obi denotes a woman's broad belt. Cinto, not Vinto, matches the following synonym cingidouro and the visible initial.
Molher identifies the belt's wearer, while muito largo describes the belt. Retain the historical o spelling in molher.

runs.text: Maneira de lençol de linho ca

lines.note: Hirazutsumi is a wrapping sheet. Lençol repairs the OCR letter error; ca begins the divided hemp term.

runs.text: nemo großo pera emburilhar as camas, &c.

lines.note: Canemo is completed and qualified as coarse, used to wrap bedding. Preserve emburilhar as printed rather than modernizing its internal order.
Hirefusu is lying prostrate. Deitarſe debruços confirms the posture and restores the missing i in Deitarſe.
Hirei is explained as rei ni arazu, lacking proper ceremony. The r/e reading in Reini is supported by that explicit Japanese etymological gloss.
Shin wa hirei wo ukezu says the deity does not accept impropriety. Corteſia completes the Portuguese pair ceremony and courtesy.

runs.text: O Cami não aceita offertas ſem as deuidas ce-

lines.note: The Portuguese makes the implication explicit: a kami does not accept offerings without due rites. Cami is embedded terminology, not Portuguese cami.
Remonias completes ceremonias and closes the ritual example. It should not be joined across physical lines in Level 1.
The second hirei is tameshi ni arazu, outside precedent or ordinary practice. It is a homonym of the preceding ritual impropriety entry.
Ordinaria and cuſtumada describe the practice that this thing is not. The apparent internal gap in the OCR is not retained as a lexical division.
Hireō or hiryō is tobu tatsu, a flying dragon. The Portuguese calls it a flying lizard; preserve that historical gloss rather than replace it with a modern zoological term.
Voa completes the flying-lizard definition. It is the predicate of lagarto above.
Hiretsu is low or inferior, explained as iyashiku otoru. Bare final t is the checked coda, not a missing tsu to add to Level 1.
Firetna supplies the adjectival form, hiretsu na hito. Idem links it to the preceding low or inferior quality.

runs.text: mem baixo, ou de eſpiritus baixos.

lines.note: The person is lowly or of low spirit. Preserve eſpiritus as printed rather than regularizing its vowel to modern Portuguese.

runs.text: Firô. Firaqi arauaſu. i, Xujinno mayeni mo

lines.note: Hirō is making something known, hiraqi arawasu. Shujin no mae ni begins the explanation of speaking before one's lord; Xujinno repairs the incoherent OCR cluster.

runs.text: Falar, ou propor ao ſenhor, ou

lines.note: Mono wo mōsu completes speaking or proposing something to a lord. The marked o in môſu is visible and expresses the long vowel.
The addressee may also be a noble person. Firôſuru is the suru verb form, not the OCR's turu.
The next hirō means fatigue, explained by tsukare and itazugawashii. Its marked o differs from the preceding announcement sense and is preserved independently.
Hirō shita means being worn out or exhausted. The example restores the headword's damaged F and vowel mark rather than reading modern romanization hiro.

runs.text: ¶. Item, Permet. Se diz de hum homem que

lines.note: Per met. signals a figurative extension: the term can describe a man depleted of resources. It is editorial Portuguese, not Japanese.

runs.text: eſtà pobre, & desfeito do fato, & riquezas

lines.note: Poverty and loss of possessions explain that figurative exhaustion. Desfeito is one printed word here, unlike OCR's split form.
Que tinha refers to the possessions and wealth the person formerly had. It closes the depleted-resources sense.
Hiroba is a broad place and, in the continuation, a public place. The damaged initial word is confirmed by the next column's Hirobaye example.
Blico completes publico across the column break. Hiroba ye de-tsuketa introduces a person accustomed to appearing in public.
Tsuketa completes de-tsuketa. The gloss describes familiarity with going out before others, not merely arriving once.
Public appearances or gatherings complete the description of that accustomed person. Preserve the Portuguese ajuntamento form.
Hirobiro to means very spacious or broadly. The repeated example begins at the line's right edge.
Hirobiro to shita koto describes a broad or extended thing. The unusual koto is preserved rather than replaced by expected mono.
Eſtendida completes the two qualities, broad and spread out. This is the end of the adverbial example.
Hirobuta is a broad cover or tray. The headword's o and Cubertura's b are visible despite damage; the next line explains its use.

runs.text: que poem veſtidos, ou outras couſas.

lines.note: Clothes or other things are placed on it. The apparent qu is left as printed rather than expanded to que without evidence.

runs.text: Firocu. Cacuxi, xiruſu. i, Daijino rocu.

lines.note: Hiroku is a secret record: kakushi shirusu, with daiji no roku as a paraphrase. The punctuation separates explanatory Japanese components.

runs.text: Liuro de grandes ſegredos, ou miſterios.

lines.note: A book of great secrets or mysteries confirms the hi-roku analysis. The translation is about contents, not the book's physical size.
Hirogaru is becoming broader or spreading. The past ending atta is restored from the damaged type, not left as impossible acta.
Kuchi ga hirogaru or suboru describes opening versus narrowing the mouth. The next example explicitly illustrates vowel pronunciation.

runs.text: Abrirſe a boca, ou fecharſe na pronunciaçaõ

lines.note: The gloss concerns opening or closing the mouth in pronunciation. Fecharſe repairs the OCR j without changing the reflexive construction.
Mǒ to yū koto wa hirogaru illustrates an open long o: the mouth opens in pronouncing Mǒ. The second enlarged pass confirms the caron on yǔ as well as the caron on Mǒ; neither is a nasal tilde.
Mô to yū koto wa suboru gives the contrasting closed long o, with the mouth narrowed. Preserve the contrast Mǒ/Mô across these two physical lines; yǔ has a caron in both examples.
Hirogeru is the transitive counterpart, widening or extending something. Its ending uru is recorded separately from the stem.
Hiroi means broad or spacious. Hiroi at the end begins a figurative example of a generous disposition.
Hiroi kokoro or ki denotes generosity. Qi is ki, not qu; condição liberal confirms the character trait rather than physical area.
Firoſa is the derived noun, breadth. The damaged o belongs to hiroi and should not yield hiresa.
Firô is the contracted adverbial derivative of hiroi. The scan shows a circumflex; preserve it independently of the picking-up verb below.
Hirō here means picking something up from the ground. Couſa restores the damaged vowel in the Portuguese object.
Takigi wo hirō means gathering firewood. The scan's circumflex is retained in the repeated verb.
Konomi wo hirō means picking fruit or nuts from the ground. The following chão completes the source-location phrase.

runs.text: chão. ¶ Item, Achar a caſo algũa couſa.

lines.note: A further sense is finding something by chance. This extends the picking-up verb, not the broadness adjective.
Kane nado wo hirō is finding money or similar things. The Portuguese silver example continues across pra-ta.
Ta completes prata, followed by other things one might find. The physical division is preserved.
Hiroiatsumeru means gathering by picking things up. The compound's first element is hiroi, not the adjective hiroi in this context.
Polo chão specifies gathering from the ground. It completes the compound verb's definition.

runs.text: Enjeitado que ſe acha em algũa parte.

lines.note: Hiroigo is a foundling, a child found abandoned somewhere. Enjeitado gives the social rather than literal picked-up-object sense.

runs.text: Couſa que hum acha a caſo, &

lines.note: Hiroimono is a thing found by chance. Hum is the generic finder, not the OCR's ham.
Toma completes finding and taking the object. It is part of the definition, not a new command.
Firǒjin is a person depleted of possessions. It relates to the exhaustion or poverty sense of hirō in column 1, not to hiroi-mono.
Yas completes alfayas, household goods or possessions. The continuation closes the poverty description.
Hirōjō is a letter presented through an intermediary, equated with atejō or tsukejō. The first o has a circumflex and jō a caron in the scan.

runs.text: vai encaminhada a peßoa que hade falar, apreſẽ

lines.note: The letter goes to someone who will speak and present it. Apreſẽ begins the divided presentation verb.

runs.text: tar eſta carta, &c. posto q̃ por reuerencia não

lines.note: The intermediary presents the letter because respect discourages direct address. Posto que introduces that qualification.

runs.text: vai direitamente dirigida ao ſenhor, ou a peſ-

lines.note: It is not directly addressed to the lord or principal person. Preserve direitamente as the printed adverb.
Soa completes peſsoa principal. This closes the account of the intermediary letter.

runs.text: Tomar o que eſtà no chão.

lines.note: Hiroitoru is taking what lies on the ground. Its toru component makes the compound distinct from simply finding something.
Hiroma is a large hall or room. The damaged F is supported by the scan and the room gloss.
Hiromaru is becoming broad or extended. The missing final i in the citation form Firomari is restored.
A law or sect can also spread. This figurative extension links physical expansion to dissemination.
Hiromariwataru means spreading widely through many places. Diuulgarſe restores the dropped u in the Portuguese verb.
Tas completes muitas partes, specifying the wide geographical spread. It belongs to the compound entry above.
Hirome is the dissemination of a law or teaching. It is the noun preceding the related transitive verb.
Hiromeru means making something broader or extending it. The initial vowel is i, not OCR's a.
The additional sense is promulgating: go-okite wo hi-romuru concerns proclaiming a regulation. Both Promulgar and Govoqiteuo are restored from the scan.
Printed catchword anticipating the opening of f198; verified against that scan. Preserved outside body text with its original stable ID.
